#10312. Are school phone bans working so far? Here’s what early studies show

The argument for school cellphone bans is simple: Phones offer endless distraction. Take them away and students can focus on classwork, engage with peers and, ultimately, learn more.

But the reality is more complicated, as emerging research shows. Schools can lock phones away in pouches or banish them to backpacks, but they can’t shut out the digital world.

In the past few years, more than 40 U.S. states have passed laws that restrict cellphones at schools, according to the Phone Free Schools State Report Card, which tracks state phone legislation. But those laws vary widely and often let schools design their own policies, resulting in a patchwork of rules and enforcement across the country.

A large-scale study published Tuesday found strict cellphone restrictions — ones that require students to put phones in locked pouches for the entire school day — result in small academic gains. But, the researchers said, the gains can add up if schools continue banning phones.

Phone bans appear to help, to a point

The study, led by Harvard’s Center for Education Policy Research, found the schools with strict phone restrictions saw “modest” improvements in academic growth, compared with students in similar schools without those restrictions. The study, which analyzed test scores of 3.3 million students at 4,600 schools nationally, estimates the academic gains were equivalent to about an additional week or two of learning over a school year.

Student achievement has been falling globally since 2013, which is roughly when social media-enabled smartphones took off. The researchers sought to determine if the decline is being reversed now that schools have started taking phones away, said Harvard professor Thomas Kane, one of the study’s authors.

“Our answer is yes, phone bans do have a positive effect on growth. But it’s not a panacea,” Kane said. Learning loss was gradual over a decade, he notes, and it’s not surprising that gains would also be gradual. The study used math and reading test data for grades four through 10 from the past five academic years.

“While schools should not expect large boosts in achievement immediately, storing students’ phones seems to be a cost-effective way to add 1-2 weeks of instruction each year, which could add up over time, just as the initial declines did,” the study says.

The boost is equal to about half the annual decline in test scores since smartphones became mainstream, the study said.

Academic gains are overall ‘disappointing,’ one researcher says

Still, the connection between phones and learning is not clear-cut.

A different study published in May concluded strict school phone bans had “close to zero” effect on test scores. It compared schools with bans with tens of thousands of other schools.

The National Bureau of Economic Research study looked at a different set of standardized test scores than Harvard’s study, as well as GPS phone activity, teacher surveys and data from Yondr, the leading provider of lockable phone pouches, at 4,600 schools that use the pouches.

The study had found “modest positive effects” in high school test scores over three years, particularly in math. But the report’s authors, researchers at Stanford, the University of Michigan, Duke and the University of Pennsylvania, were hesitant to conclude overall learning benefits from the bans.

Both studies point to a similar conclusion, said Stanford education economist Thomas Dee, an author of the NBER study. “The early results from school phone bans are largely disappointing and raise unresolved questions,” Dee said.

Noting that the Harvard study showed learning gains may accumulate over time, Dee said: “I hope they’re right. However, I’m not comfortable making that extrapolation from estimates that are small, sensitive and based on just a few years of phone bans.”

The reasons, Dee said, could be that students are still distracted on other devices at school. Or, he said, “it may be that we see these disappointing results because out-of-school phone use is harming child development.”

Phones aren’t the only tech distracting teens

Just because schools or states have phone bans does not mean they’re being enforced, said Jean Twenge, a psychologist at San Diego State University and author of “10 Rules for Raising Kids in a High-Tech World.”

Ask any teacher — or teenager — and they’ll tell you that some phone bans are largely cosmetic. Teens come up with creative workarounds, including stowing burner phones or even phone-shaped rocks in their locked pouches. At schools that rely on students to keep phones in backpacks, adherence to the ban can be spotty.

“It happens pretty often that there’s a policy of no phones during the school day, bell-to-bell, and you go into the school and phones are everywhere,” Twenge said.

Even without phones, “Do they have laptops at school? Are they just doing social media on laptops instead?” Twenge said.

Phone use outside of school affects academics too, Twenge said. “If they have that phone available when they’re studying, how much are they really taking in?”

Kane, of the Harvard study, agrees the effect of cellphone use outside of school is “the big question.” But researchers have not been able to investigate parents and educators’ suspicions that late-night binges on YouTube and other platforms are costly for students.

“I find it astonishing that social media companies know how much time kids spend on their platforms, but that data has never been linked to student outcomes,” Kane said. “We can’t provide answers until the social media companies share data.”

—Jocelyn Gecker, AP Education Writer

#10309. Top 6 AI Text to Speech Tools in 2026: Features, Strengths and Limits

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Not long ago, a synthetic voice was easy to spot: flat, rushed and strangely stressed. Today, the best AI text to speech tools can read a script with natural pacing, switch accents, whisper or laugh on cue, and even speak in a voice cloned from a short recording. That makes them useful far beyond screen readers. Developers use them for product voice prompts, marketers for video voiceovers, teachers for course narration and writers for listening back to their own drafts.

This guide explains how modern text-to-speech works, what to look for when choosing a tool, and compares six options: OpenArt, ElevenLabs, Murf AI, Speechify, WellSaid Labs and Amazon Polly. Each section covers strengths, limits and the best use case. The details come from each vendor’s own pages at the time of writing, and plans, models and prices change often, so confirm current terms before you commit.

OpenArt’s AI text to speech tool lives inside a wider creative platform. You open the Audio tab, choose Create voice-over, select a model, paste your script, pick a voice, generate, listen and download. It runs in the browser with nothing to install. According to OpenArt’s page, you can switch between models for each script, including Fish Audio Drama 3, Eleven v4 and Eleven v4 Turbo.

The direction system is what makes it practical for storytelling. You add notes in square brackets, such as [whispering], [laughs] or [pause], directly in the script. OpenArt says Fish Audio Drama 3 gives close control over single words and mid-line changes of mood, while Eleven v4 reads the whole script to infer the emotion of each line and keeps the voice steady when you regenerate a line. Preset voices are labeled by accent, gender and age, and you can upload a recording of your own voice to clone it.

Because OpenArt also makes video and background music, you can build the voiceover, visuals and soundtrack in one place. It describes a Director mode for planning stories up to five minutes, and the voiceover can also be added in any video editor.

Pricing: New accounts get 40 free credits. Paid plans add monthly credits and watermark-free downloads, and commercial rights apply on eligible paid plans. Check the pricing page for current plans.

Best for: creators who want expressive voiceovers together with AI video and music.

ElevenLabs is one of the best-known names in AI voice. Its text to speech page describes a large voice library, voice design and both instant and professional voice cloning, with the latest model, Eleven v4, positioned as the most expressive. It also lists Eleven v3, Multilingual v2 and a low-latency Flash and Turbo family aimed at real-time use, and it claims support for more than 90 languages and accents, with the exact count varying by model.

For developers, there is a text to speech API with SDKs, which makes it practical for apps, games, agents and automated pipelines. The free plan includes 10,000 credits a month, and paid plans start with Starter at $6 a month, then Creator at $22 and Pro at $99, according to the vendor page, with introductory offers on the first month.

Pricing: Free plan with 10,000 credits a month. Paid plans from $6 a month as listed on the vendor page.

Best for: expressive narration, multilingual content and apps that need a voice API.

Murf AI positions itself as a studio for voiceovers. Its page lists more than 200 voices, built with permission and partnership from professional voice actors who earn royalties, and support for 35 or more languages for text to speech, with dubbing in 40 or more. The Studio editor offers pitch, speed and intonation controls and a custom pronunciation library, which helps with brand names and technical terms.

Murf also has an API. Its page describes Falcon 2 for conversational use with time-to-first-audio under 100 milliseconds, priced at $0.01 per minute, and Gen 2 for controllable voiceovers. Gen 2’s “Say it My Way” feature lets you record your own rendition so the model reflects your tone and inflections.

Pricing: Free plan with limits. Paid plan prices are on Murf’s pricing page.

Best for: marketing videos, training and presentations where you want to fine-tune delivery.

Speechify is built around reading aloud. You paste text or upload a PDF, DOCX, TXT or EPUB file, pick a voice, adjust playback speed and listen or download the audio. Its page lists more than 1,000 voices across 60 or more languages, including several regional English accents, and the tool works in the browser and in apps for iOS, Android, Mac and Windows, plus Chrome and Edge extensions.

The use cases lean toward productivity and accessibility: studying, going through emails and documents, language learning and support for people with visual impairments, dyslexia or ADHD. A free account saves your documents and syncs them across devices.

Pricing: You can start free. Paid plans are listed on Speechify’s pricing page.

Best for: students, professionals and anyone who wants to listen to documents and articles.

WellSaid Labs focuses on professional voiceover for businesses. Every voice is built from recordings of a real voice actor who consented and is paid when the voice is used, and the voices are licensed for commercial use. Its page describes hundreds of voices across languages, accents, tones and styles.

Pronunciation control is a highlight. You can highlight a word to see suggested pronunciations and save your choice to a team library that applies to every project, and set pacing, emphasis and pronunciation line by line. WellSaid also describes a Producer product that connects AI assistants to WellSaid through MCP and its API.

Pricing: Contact sales for a quote based on your voiceover volume.

Best for: corporate training, product marketing, courses and advertising where licensing and consistency matter.

Amazon Polly is Amazon Web Services’ text to speech service, and it is aimed squarely at developers. According to AWS, it supports more than 40 languages and language variants with over 100 male and female voices, and it works through APIs in your code. It supports SSML, the W3C standard markup for phrasing, emphasis and intonation, and custom lexicons that fix the pronunciation of acronyms and terms. Output formats include MP3 and OGG.

Pricing is usage-based. AWS lists a free tier for new accounts, with usage allowances that depend on the voice engine, so estimate your character volume before you decide. A short example shows how little code a basic request takes:

The sample uses the AWS SDK for JavaScript, calls the neural engine and sends SSML so that the pause and emphasis are explicit. Adjust the region, voice and engine to match what your account supports.

Pricing: Usage-based with a free tier for new accounts. See the AWS pricing page for current rates.

Best for: apps, IVR systems, notifications and any product that needs automated speech at scale.

Treat this table as a starting point. Features and limits change often, so test two or three tools with the same script.

Modern text-to-speech systems turn written words into audio through several stages.

Newer expressive systems go further by reading the whole script to infer emotion and context, and by accepting direction in the text itself, such as a bracketed note that says to whisper. That is why a single script can produce very different reads depending on the model and the instructions.

If you use a tool with SSML support, you can make a spoken code or number far clearer:

The say-as element tells the engine to read the number digit by digit, and the break and emphasis tags shape the rhythm. Supported tags and attributes differ between engines, so check the documentation for yours.

What is the best AI text to speech tool? It depends on the job. OpenArt suits voiceovers with video and music, ElevenLabs suits expressive multilingual audio, Murf AI suits studio-style control, Speechify suits listening, WellSaid Labs suits licensed corporate work and Amazon Polly suits developers.

Is AI text to speech free? Several tools offer free plans or credits, but limits are common. Examples include OpenArt’s free credits for new accounts, ElevenLabs’ free monthly credits and Murf’s limited free plan, which has no commercial licence.

Can I use AI voices commercially? Often yes on paid plans, but the rules differ by tool. Always check the current licence before publishing.

Can AI text to speech clone my voice? Some tools support it, including OpenArt and ElevenLabs, usually from a short recording of your own voice. Only clone voices you have permission to use.

What is SSML? Speech Synthesis Markup Language is a W3C standard that lets you control pauses, emphasis, pronunciation and pitch in synthetic speech. Amazon Polly is one service that supports it.

Which tool is best for developers? Amazon Polly and ElevenLabs both offer APIs, and Murf describes API options as well. Evaluate latency, languages, pricing and SDK support for your use case.

How do I make AI voices sound less robotic? Write conversationally, add pauses and emphasis, correct pronunciations and split long scripts into short sections. Choose a model that is designed for expressive reads.

AI text to speech is now good enough for real projects, but the right tool depends on what you are making. OpenArt is a strong first stop for expressive voiceovers alongside video and music, ElevenLabs offers a deep voice library and API, Murf AI and WellSaid Labs suit polished, controlled narration, Speechify turns documents into audio and Amazon Polly fits straight into developer workflows. Test two or three with your own script, check the licence and always listen to the full result before it goes live.

#10307. Here’s how high achievers self-sabotage their goals

We’re getting close to the end of the year, and if you’re an ambitious individual, you might have your new year’s goals on your mind. You might be thinking about what goals you want to commit to for the year ahead, and assessing your progress toward the goals that you set for yourself at the beginning of the year.

And if you find yourself not making as much progress as you would have liked, it might be tempting to give up on the goal altogether. After all, there isn’t that long to go until January 1. What’s the point of continuing to work on it if you’re not sure whether you can complete it 100% by the end of the year? 

If you find yourself with these kinds of thoughts in your head, you might just be suffering from a mindset that is preventing you from making major progress on your goals. 

Where “all-or-nothing” thinking comes from 

That mindset is an “all-or-nothing” approach—where you view situations and circumstances in absolute terms, with no nuance or middle ground. An all-or-nothing mindset can manifest in different ways. In goal-setting, it can look like reviewing your week, month, or year, and looking back at the times you faltered or struggled and telling yourself some versions of “I did terrible this week” or “I blew it,” says Allison Niebes-Davis, a licensed psychologist who runs a practice in Downers Grove, Illinois.  

Niebes-Davis explains that our brains are constantly making meaning of the things around us. It can do so quickly and efficiently as a survival tool. “The problem is that when the brain is doing that, it doesn’t always do that accurately. And so sometimes when it is trying to make meaning and draw conclusions, it doesn’t always draw the most accurate conclusions or the most nuanced conclusions,” she says. 

Many high-achievers might struggle with this mindset, Niebes-Davis explains, because they can have a dichotomous way of seeing themselves. “Sometimes, high-achievers can be very self-critical, and so they use a lot of words like failure, success, win, and lose.” Because of this, they “think that they will motivate themselves by seeing things in that all-or-nothing mindset,” she continues. 

How the mindset sabotages your goals

For high-achievers, this mindset might have worked in the past, or even in other areas of their lives. This is true for Erica Dhawan, author, keynote speaker, and advisor to CEOs and leaders. Dhawan has ticked off many goals she set for herself this year—from family to keynote speeches. But she found herself struggling with her weight goals. She noticed an all-or-nothing approach creeping in when she had growth and setbacks. “I do get into a wave of good health, but then when I lose it, I don’t fall back on progress. I’m known as an ambitious, high-achieving person who gets a lot done. I also wonder if all-or-nothing is perfectionism, where I do achieve the perfect goal in certain areas, and I don’t in others,” Dhawan reflects. 

Niebes-Davis stresses that while the all-or-nothing mindset can push some people toward success, it’s unlikely to be an approach that is healthy and sustainable in the long run. “Our thoughts and emotions are so directly connected,” she says. The path to achieving a goal is “rarely linear,” says Niebes-Davis, and “nobody’s getting 100%, 100% of the time.” If the only way you can describe something is success and failure, she says, you’ll end up seeing struggles and setbacks as failures. 

“That doesn’t motivate anyone to keep working or to keep trying,” she continues.  

The importance of language 

Both Niebes-Davis and Dhawan say that culture can also encourage this type of thinking. Social media, says Dhawan, gives us “picture perfect” images that can condition us into thinking anything less isn’t good enough. This has also created a culture where “we struggle so much in our current day with nuance. Things are either/or. They’re in extremes. We don’t teach kids from a young age about how to have more nuanced language.”

Niebes-Davis says that rather than the overly rigid language we often use when we fall short, it’s more accurate to say things like “I struggled around these three things. This month was hard. I made some choices that were not in line with my goals.”

A better approach  

Adopting this kind of language in your goal-setting approach, says Niebes-Davis, shifts your mindset toward prioritizing progress rather than an arbitrary outcome. She gives the example of someone who, like Dhawan, has a goal to be at a specific weight. Say that person’s goal is to lose ten pounds. “If you’re only going to give yourself credit or positive reinforcement when you lose ten pounds,” she says, “what happens at one pound? Two pounds? Three pounds?”

Being able to celebrate smaller progress, says Niebes-Davis, gives you the option to “look at things from a data-driven mindset.” That means tracking smaller things and paying attention to what moves the needle. That way, if you find yourself having a week where you ended up gaining a pound, you’re more likely to assess the situation accurately and, in turn, make the necessary changes. “Maybe you made some choices that weren’t super in line with your goals,” she says. You can then course-correct and get back on track rather than giving up on your goals altogether. 

Focusing on process, habits and progress 

Niebes-Davis also recommends that individuals focus on process rather than outcomes. Rather than just tracking outcomes, she recommends people ask themselves, “What are the processes that would contribute to movement around that goal?” She acknowledges that this is harder to do, and is something that we don’t see often. “When we look at people and their progress toward their goals, we tend to really see and celebrate that outcome-based approach.” 

This is a practice that Dhawan is committing to. Rather than giving up on her all-or-nothing weight goal, she’s committed to practicing healthy habits until the end of the year. That might mean eliminating alcohol and sugar, writing for 30 minutes, or meditating every morning. 

Moving away from the all-or-nothing mindset, says Niebes-Davis, is ultimately about training ourselves as humans. “We tend to give greater attention to the things that we struggle with, or the times we didn’t align with our goals. So a lot of being able to move the needle is to be very intentional about recognizing the successes.” 

She continues, “That takes work, and that takes intention, but that is going to put us in a much healthier place for goals, relationships, health and all of that.”

#10305. Shopping for a tween? These gifts won’t get an eye roll

Buying a gift for a tween is a risky endeavor. Nail it, and you’re a legend. Miss, and you’ll get an eyeroll.

Tweens live in a tricky in-between zone. They’ve outgrown the kids’ section, but they’re not ready for the adult aisle. For the last decade, brands weren’t much help, as magazines and clothing labels targeted to this age group went out of business.

But this holiday season, tweens are back in the spotlight. A wave of startups is making clothes and skincare for kids ages 7 to 14. Claire’s is reinventing itself. Print magazines are making a comeback. Even the phone is being reimagined for them.

For this year’s guide, I went looking for gifts that hit the sweet spot. These products are mature enough to feel like a step forward without pushing kids to grow up before they’re ready. Many of them also lure kids off their screens and back into the real world.

Each of these gifts had to win over both the tween who unwraps it and the parent who pays for it.

Print is back

Anyway, Annual Magazine Subscription, $40

If you grew up taking quizzes in YM to find out which Spice Girl you were, you already understand the magic of the tween magazine. Anyway is a new print magazine for kids ages 9 to 15. It covers the awkward issues that can feel mortifying to ask about (crushes, body odor), along with style and culture. Every issue comes with a sticker sheet, a comic, and other screen-free activities.

A suitcase for jet setters in training

Away, The Carry-On in Misty Purple, $278; Featherlight Daily Backpack in Misty Purple, $98

Away built its suitcases for millennial travelers. Now those millennials have tween children, and those tweens want luggage of their own. This summer, Away launched In Between, a collection designed for this age group. The Carry-On is the brand’s classic hard-shell suitcase but sized slightly smaller than its adult version, and slightly bigger than its kids’ product. It even has room for a monogram of up to three letters. You can also get a matching backpack that slides right over the suitcase handle; it has a laptop sleeve, a water bottle pocket, and a D-ring for bag charms.

Her first fragrance

Evereden, Hair and Body Fragrance Mist Trio, $72

The first signature scent is a rite of passage. (I admit, I doused myself in Anna Sui’s Sui Dreams before the school dance.) Evereden’s trio of hair and body mists is formulated for kids and teens ages 6 and up, without phthalates, parabens, or common fragrance allergens. The scents have great names—Main Character, Darling, and Supernova—or whoever your tween wants to be that day.

GRWM: Holiday edition

Bubble, Main Attraction Hydrating Super Set, $70

After hordes of tweens took over Sephora, parents became wary of their kids’ slathering on harsh anti-aging serums meant for women decades older. So it’s comforting that Bubble designs skincare products specifically for the needs of young skin, namely moisture. The Main Attraction set packs six of the brand’s favorites into a festive travel bag, including Soft Launch cream cleanser, Cosmic Silk milky toner, Water Slide serum, Power Wave moisturizer, and Talk Back lip serum. The formulas use gentle, hydrating ingredients like hyaluronic acid and shea butter.

The hallway status symbol, upgraded

Lululemon, Everywhere Belt Bag with Long Strap 1.3L, $44

If middle school has an official uniform, the Lululemon belt bag is part of it. This year, the brand gave the original a makeover. The strap now detaches with hidden snaps, and the main zipper clips into a little paracord loop as an extra safety feature. It’s big enough for a phone, lip balm, and emergency snacks, and comes in an array of colors—like lavender and fuchsia—that tweens will love.

Screen-free relaxation

Lifelines, FlowArt Dot-By-Letter, Landscapes, $12.99

Between homework, after-school activities, and friend drama, tween life can be overwhelming. With FlowArt, kids can decompress without a screen. It works by allowing them to create landscapes using tiny dots. Each pad has 20 scenes and comes with four double-sided markers in eight colors, along with a tray to keep them in, so they don’t get lost in a bag. At under $15, it’s a perfect stocking stuffer.

A first phone parents will approve of

Freckle, $199, plus $25 per month for service

If you’re looking to give your kid independence but are wary of giving them a smartphone, you’re in luck. Freckle, which I wrote about this fall, is a phone for kids 7 to 13 that skips the browser, the app store, social media, and YouTube. Instead, it has a camera that identifies bugs, birds, and plants and saves them to a digital sticker book. Kids can call and text approved contacts, and two Freckles tapped together turn into walkie-talkies. There’s even a tap-to-pay wallet for pocket money. The first batch ships in December, so preorder soon if you want one under the tree.

A Monthly Build Box

CrunchLabs, Build Box Subscription, $329.40 per year

There’s a good chance your tween already worships Mark Rober, the former NASA engineer whose YouTube experiments include glitter bombs for package thieves and obstacle courses for squirrels. He’s launched a subscription box called CrunchLabs with a new build-it-yourself toy that arrives every month. Past builds include a coin-snatching machine, a disc launcher, and a drawing robot, and each is linked to a 15- to 30-minute video of Rober explaining the engineering behind it. The kits are designed so kids 8 to 13 can finish them on their own in an afternoon, and then spend hours playing with what they made. It’s also available month to month for $29.95 a box. Kids 14 and up can graduate to the Hack Pack, which adds coding and robotics.

Make Your Legos Move

LEGO Education, Computer Science & AI Kit, $429.95 (grades 3–5) or $529.95 (grades 6–8)

LEGO’s new kit allows kids to build machines, and in doing so, teach themselves the basics of robotics and AI. The kits come with the LEGO bricks your child has played with their whole life, but thanks to motors and sensors, they can create machines and robots that can move. The system is designed to teach coding basics in a fun way. LEGO is careful about keeping data private. No data is transferred to the company, kids don’t have log-ins of their own, and all projects are saved locally. The grades 3–5 kit suits younger tweens, and the grades 6–8 kit adds an extra motor and a controller for kids 11 and up.

The Claire’s comeback collection

Claire’s, Disney Villains Earring Stack, $29.99, and Faux Gel Nails, $19.99

Claire’s, the last survivor of the ’90s mall, is staging a comeback, with new owners and redesigned stores. Its exclusive Disney Villains collection of accessories and cosmetics features Ursula, Maleficent, the Evil Queen, or Cruella De Vil in matching earring stacks, fragrances, and faux gel nails. Tweens gravitate towards villains because they are still part of the Disney world, but they are too cool to feel babyish. If you want to make it an experience, you can pair the earrings with a trip to Claire’s for a new piercing.

Beautiful books

Juniper Books, Harry Potter Mashup Book Set, $424.99

The bookshelf is the new status symbol, and this set is a showstopper. Juniper Books wraps all seven Harry Potter hardcover editions in custom jackets that serve as decor in a tween’s room. On a shelf, the spines form a single design that blends the colors and symbols of each of the four Hogwarts houses. It’s definitely a splurge, but it is likely to be on the shelf long after they’ve outgrown many of the items on this list.

A party dress

Pleat, Ruby Dress, $72

Sara Fowler, founder of Pleat, started the brand because she couldn’t find anything for tween girls between the smocked dress and the crop top. The Ruby Dress is one of Pleat’s most popular styles. Soft pleats gather at the neckline above a bloused top, and a fitted waist gives just a hint of shape without hugging the body. It comes in a silky fabric in teal, dark green, red, and a Forget Me Nots print, in sizes 7 to 16. It’s festive enough for a holiday concert, family dinner, and New Year’s Eve.

The sleepover flex

Buttah London, The Button Me Up Lounge Set, £99 (about $130)

It’s sleepover season, and tweens are often stressed about what to pack when they’re invited to a friend’s house. London-based Buttah has created a just-right lounge set for the occasion. It features a long-sleeve top with nice details like ruching and heart embroidery. It’s cropped, but it lands right at the waistband, so there’s no midriff showing, which parents will appreciate. It pairs with wide-leg pants that have a contrasting bow.

SpaceX's Elon Musk and Epic Games' Tim Sweeney are two of Huang's biggest cheerleaders in an attempt to get him his job back.

Just days after he left the company under a cloud of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang might be on his way back to the company he founded. That's after a number of his allies rallied in support for Huang, including influential SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and outspoken Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney. The pair are just two of those demanding that Nvidia's board has a rethink, hoping that it will choose to "Bring Jensen Back" to the company. Huang is now discussing that possibility, according to a Financial Times report.

"Huang has discussed with confidantes the possibility of returning, according to multiple people familiar with the matter," the report claimed, adding that allies were putting together a "war room" of Silicon Valley figures to try and lobby for his return.

Huang's resignation from his Nvidia post came after he released a statement confirming his affair, one which could have repercussions far beyond Nvidia itself. U.S. intelligence was reported to believe that the woman involved in an affair with Jensen Huang, Alice Huang (no relation), is a spy working for the Chinese Ministry of State Security, or MSS. Ms. Huang was an executive at Megaspeed, an AI company accused of smuggling $2 billion worth of AI chips into China via a subsidiary called Speedmatrix. Since Jensen Huang admitted to his adultery, it was further alleged that he had a second affair, this time with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. That alone would potentially constitute a violation of Nvidia's own code of conduct. But the affair with an alleged Chinese spy is likely to be the most troublesome for the former-but-potentially-returning CEO.

Now, an open letter sent to Nvidia's board by Huang's allies has urged them to leave “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.” The open letter was penned by Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker, both shareholders.

@yunta_tsai A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I’m signing it tooNovember 13, 2026

However, Nvidia has already started looking elsewhere. After placing chief financial officer Colette Kress in charge on an interim basis, it's believed the company has approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas as a potential Huang successor. Haas spent around seven years at Nvidia before leaving in 2013, but no official confirmation has been announced, nor is it likely to be until a decision is made.

It's possible that Huang can expect a vote of confidence from U.S. President Donald Trump, with the pair having a good relationship to date. But Trump recently called for former Apple CEO Tim Cook to take over at Nvidia.

Outside of the White House, Huang has other concerns to deal with. Congress has summoned him to appear before a Select Committee over his affair with the suspected Chinese spy, threatening to subpoena him if necessary.

#10302. This is the wrong reason to claim Social Security benefits early

YouTube creator Erin Moriarity recently appeared on Morningstar’s The Long View podcast. She spoke with podcast hosts Christine Benz and Amy Arnott about why she feels positive about the future of Social Security benefits; her advice for young people planning for retirement; and Social Security mistakes to watch out for.

You like to push back on concerns about the future of Social Security. Can you explain why you think that people who are, say, over 50 should feel some comfort that their promised benefits will be there for them?

MORIARITY: People over 50 vote, and those in Congress know it. If they upset that population, it’s not going to go well for them. They’re going to lose their job. I think Congress has a huge motivation to act. I do think Social Security will experience reform and will see changes. I don’t necessarily know what those changes would be, whether it’s reducing cost-of-living adjustments going forward, increasing the wage cap. I mean, there might be the potential that they try to borrow in order to fund the trust fund, which we’ve never done before. They would have to rewrite the laws, but there’s going to be a way in which they keep Social Security going forward. And I think people over 50 don’t have to worry about changes to their benefits. I think people in my generation, 30s, I think benefits will change, but benefits will be there.

The narrative is often that Social Security is going bankrupt, and that’s not true. There are current workers today who are paying into the system, and that pays out to the current retirees today. It would still be able to pay out what’s coming in, which currently is about 77% of what the payouts would be, but I don’t think benefits would be cut for near-term or current retirees.

As a younger person trying to plan for retirement, would you assume that future Social Security benefits might be reduced, or how would you handle those potential changes?

MORIARITY: If I’m talking to somebody who’s in their 20s, 30s, or even their early 40s, I don’t even want them considering Social Security at that point. Not that I don’t think it’s going to be there; I think it will be, but I want you saving and investing in a way where you’re not relying on it because I’d rather you get to retirement and say, oh, I have more than enough, or I can potentially retire early, or I can take extra vacations that I didn’t think I was going to. It’s a better position to get to retirement and have more money rather than less.

I think once you get to your late 40s and 50s, and especially in your 60s, I mean, you’re already at Social Security age—I would look at what those benefits are. I’d build my budget, figure out what my gap is between what Social Security is and how much I want to spend. But prior to 45 or something, save and invest as if you’re kind of blind to what those Social Security benefits would be.

What are the big Social Security pitfalls or mistakes that people should be aware of?

MORIARITY: I think one of the biggest is one we already touched on: Thinking that the trust fund is going to be totally depleted, meaning that there wouldn’t be benefits for you or that your benefits would be cut. I hear so many people right now saying, “Claim as early as you can so you can get something while it’s there.” And I just think that that’s a fearful mentality. The more we operate out of fear, the worse decisions we tend to make. I think if I look back over the course of my life, I have not made great decisions if I made them out of fear.

I would bring it back to what my budget looks like, what my portfolio looks like, and really, how much security do I need? There’s great value in having a reliable income stream that is inflation-adjusted for the remainder of your life.

Build around what you truly need in your plan, in your budget, and look at what you might need for the next couple of decades, and truly look at what size portfolio you have and what kind of gap you can fill, and make your decision based on that.

If you’re married, factor in that one of you is going to pass away first. It makes a lot of sense in many cases to have the higher-earning spouse delay because whoever (survives), they get to keep the higher earner’s benefit, and that can provide a lot of security to the surviving spouse.

This edited Q&A was provided to The Associated Press by Morningstar. For more retirement content, go to https://www.morningstar.com/retirement.

Christine Benz is director of personal finance and retirement planning for Morningstar and co-host of The Long View podcast. Subscribe to her free newsletter, Improving Your Finances.

Amy C. Arnott, CFA, is a portfolio strategist for Morningstar and co-host of The Long View podcast.

#10300. Data-Driven Pages That Never Go Stale: A Practical Guide

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every developer has shipped the other kind of page: a lovingly written article or landing page that peaks on launch day and then quietly rots. Screenshots age, statistics expire, rankings slide. Data-driven pages play the opposite game. Built from a living dataset, they republish themselves daily, grow to thousands of URLs, and answer questions nobody had asked when the site launched. This guide breaks down how they work, using a real fan-run stats site as the running example: one public dataset in, more than ten thousand fresh pages out.

Static pages lose ground because the web moves and they do not. Facts expire, competitors publish fresher answers, and search engines reward pages whose information matches today. A page that cannot update itself must be rewritten by hand, so most sites update a few pages and abandon the rest.

Freshness is not one rule for the whole web; it depends on the query. Nobody needs a CSS tutorial rewritten weekly, but statistics, prices, availability and anything with a season attached decays on a schedule. Developers misjudge this constantly, treating every page like documentation when half their catalogue is really a perishable good. Serve a three-month-old stat as if it were current and readers learn the most damaging lesson a site can teach: do not trust the numbers here.

Then there is the maintenance maths. A hundred hand-written pages each needing one review a year is a hundred small debts, and the interest compounds as the catalogue grows. The team updates the flagship pages, promises to return for the rest, and quietly never does. Data-driven architecture is really a staffing decision disguised as a technical one: humans design the system once, and the system does the updating forever.

A data-driven site has three layers: a dataset that refreshes on a schedule, templates that turn records into pages, and URL patterns that map every meaningful combination users might search for. Change the data and every page changes; improve a template and ten thousand pages improve at once.

The running example makes this concrete. A fan-built Overwatch stats tracker republishes Blizzard's public hero data on a daily cycle. From that one feed it generates hero profiles, head-to-head matchup pages and multi-condition tier lists: 10,291 URLs in its sitemap, across six languages, with matchup pages alone accounting for 8,586 of them. Nobody wrote those pages. Somebody designed the system that writes them, which is a very different, and much more scalable, job.

The example runs on Next.js behind a CDN, but the stack is the least important layer of the three. The same pipeline feeding WordPress, Astro or a static site generator would look identical from the reader's side of the glass. Choose boring technology you already know, and spend your originality budget on the dataset and the templates, because that is where readers will feel the difference.

Generated pages stay useful when every URL must earn its existence with data. Set minimum thresholds before a page is published, give each template unique modules its siblings do not have, and noindex combinations with nothing to say. The line between a resource and spam is not automation; it is emptiness.

Quality gates work best when they are public and mechanical. The example site publishes its tier formula openly: 70% of the score from win rate, 30% from pick rate, and a hard floor that excludes heroes picked in under 0.5% of matches from topping the ranking, because a tiny sample cannot prove anything. That single floor is editorial policy expressed as code. Your version might be a minimum number of data points, a minimum price history, or a minimum review count — the number matters less than the fact that the gate exists and applies to every page equally.

Each template also needs modules its siblings cannot copy. A hero profile carries a seven-day trend and its best and worst matchups; a matchup page carries the head-to-head history; a tier list carries the movement since yesterday. Add a short human layer on top — a methodology page explaining the scoring, changelogs narrating what moved — and the catalogue stops reading as output and starts reading as a publication. Google's scaled-content rules target pages manufactured to manipulate rankings with little value; a page that answers a real query with real, current data is the opposite of that. The honest test for any generated URL is simple: if it vanished tonight, would a searcher lose an answer?

Start embarrassingly small: one dataset, one entity type, one template. A football club's results archive, a property portal's sold prices, your own product catalogue — anything structured and refreshed beats a grand plan. Prove one template earns traffic, then add combinations, languages and dashboards in that order.

What is programmatic SEO? Programmatic SEO means generating many pages from a structured dataset using templates, instead of writing each page by hand. Done well, each page answers a distinct search with real data. Done badly, it produces thousands of near-identical pages, which is where its reputation suffers.

Is programmatic SEO against Google's rules? No. Google's spam policies target scaled content created mainly to manipulate rankings, with little or no value for users. Pages generated from real data that answer real queries are publishing. The deciding question is whether a page helps its reader, not how it was produced.

How often should the data behind pages refresh? Match the refresh to how fast the underlying facts change. Sports and game statistics justify daily pulls, prices often need hourly checks, and reference data may only move monthly. Refreshing faster than reality changes wastes crawl budget and makes 'updated' stamps meaningless.

Do generated pages need unique written text? They need unique value, which is not the same thing. Identical paragraphs on ten thousand pages add nothing, but unique data, comparisons and trends are content in their own right. Add short human-written context per template, and let the data carry the differences between pages.

How many pages should a first project launch with? Launch with the smallest set that proves the template: one entity type, a few hundred pages at most. Validate that search engines index them and users engage before adding combinations and languages. Scaling an unproven template just manufactures tomorrow's cleanup job at industrial size.

The sites quietly winning the long game are not publishing more; they are publishing systems. One honest dataset, one well-built template and strict quality gates will outlast a hundred hand-written pages competing on freshness alone. Try it this week: take one dataset you already own, design a single template with four real modules, and ship fifty pages. Watch what the data does next.

#10299. Nvidia earnings preview: How Jensen Huang updates could impact the stock, whether the results are strong or not

All eyes are always on Nvidia’s (Nasdaq: NVDA) earnings. The company is the backbone of the AI revolution, after all.

But today’s results—and its upcoming financial call—will be the first without cofounder and former CEO Jensen Huang at the helm, which could make this the company’s most consequential report in Nvidia’s history.

Investors will not only want to see favorable growth, but they will want an update on the company’s direction after Huang resigned amid multiple scandals last week.

And if that update doesn’t assuage fears—or if it leads to more uncertainty—the stock could continue its downward spiral. Here’s what you need to know.

Nvidia reports Q3 2027 results today

After markets close today, Nvidia will report results for its third quarter of fiscal 2027, which ended on October 25. The results are expected around 4:20 p.m. ET, with the earnings conference call scheduled to begin at 5 p.m. ET.

As far as numbers go, investors are expecting big results from Nvidia. As noted by CNBC, Wall Street analysts expect the company to report revenue of $109.1 billion and earnings per share (EPS) of $2.47. 

If Nvidia hits that revenue target, it will represent staggering growth of 91% versus the same quarter last year, when the company posted $59 billion in revenue.

However, even if Nvidia achieves 91% growth, it will be lower than the 106% YOY growth the company saw in its second quarter, when it reported $96.2 billion in revenue.

That suggests growth is slowing—something investors never like to hear. Indeed, in August, Nvidia’s then chief financial officer and current interim CEO, Colette Kress, said the company expects just 70% growth in fiscal 2028, which she attributed to a “supply constrained outlook.”

But numbers are one thing. What investors will really want to hear about is what the company plans to do in a post-Huang world.

Jensen Huang may be out, but he’s still at the top of investors’ minds

Last week, the AI world was rocked when Nvidia’s cofounder and CEO resigned amid a set of scandals.

The first scandal had to do with his affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence believed may have been spying for China. Beijing officials have strongly denied the allegations.

However, the allegations and their resulting national security concerns were enough to compromise Huang’s position at the company. Then, shortly after reports of a second alleged affair, this time with an Nvidia employee, emerged, Huang resigned as CEO.

Shortly after Huang resigned, Nvidia announced that its CFO, Colette Kress, would step into the interim chief executive role while it sought a new CEO. The company is reportedly considering both internal and external candidates.

In recent days, there have also been rumblings that Huang may be planning to make a comeback and return to the CEO role, much like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman did in 2023 after he was ousted.

Investors will want updates on both issues: how the search for Huang’s replacement is progressing and whether the board would even be open to Huang’s return.

They’ll also likely want an update on Nvidia’s internal investigation into whether the company’s secrets, or national security secrets, were compromised by Huang’s alleged affairs.

Which way will NVDA stock go?

Currently, NVDA stock is trading down about 1.2% ahead of the company’s results later today. Unfortunately for investors, that red on NVDA’s charts is par for the course as of late.

In the past five trading days alone, NVDA shares have lost more than 7.5% in value. Over the past month, shares have cratered more than 27%. 

The scandals and Huang’s departure have had an abysmal effect on Nvidia’s stock price. That fall was first exacerbated by fears that AI spending could be declining as companies start to rein in costs. The Huang scandals then acted as a pile-on.

Nvidia’s all-time closing high was $239.24 on October 6, just less than six weeks ago. At the time, the company had a valuation of more than $5.7 trillion.

But today, post-Huang scandal, the company’s share price is below $154, a level it hasn’t been at since mid-2025. The company currently has a valuation of $3.7 trillion—a fall of roughly $2 trillion.

If Nvidia’s Q3 results are stellar and the company’s new interim leadership reassures investors about its direction and future, investors could reward the stock after hours, sending it up.

But if Nvidia’s numbers don’t excite—and, more importantly, if Nvidia’s comments on Huang and the company’s future leadership don’t inspire confidence—NVDA could see more red ahead.

Intel has been sued by shareholders who accuse the company of misleading investors about the severity of the PC market downturn and its impact on the company's financial performance before its shares plunged by nearly 29% in late October, reports Reuters.

The proposed class action lawsuit led by the Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System pension fund was filed on Friday in a federal court in San Jose, California. The lawsuit alleges that Intel failed to inform investors in a timely manner about the extent to which slow demand for consumer processors and excessive inventories would affect its sales. In particular, the plaintiffs argue that the negative impact of the PC market downturn on Intel's business was greater than the benefits the company enjoyed from the unprecedented buildout of AI data center infrastructure and other AI-related opportunities.

"Intel made statements that were materially false and/or misleading when made because they failed to disclose the following adverse facts pertaining to Intel’s business," the lawsuit reads.

While Intel, like many other major technology companies, has invested heavily in its manufacturing capabilities, supply constraints have prevented the chipmaker from fully capitalizing on strong demand for data center processors. Meanwhile, a severe shortage of memory has driven up DRAM prices and, consequently, the cost of PCs, which has affected demand for consumer systems. As a result, Intel could not sell enough CPUs in the third quarter, which dramatically affected the company's stock price in October.

Intel chief executive Lip-Bu Tan expressed disappointment with the supply constraints, the extraordinary situation in the memory market, and the subsequent weakness of the PC business during the company's earnings call. Yet, the plaintiff believes that the company should have warned about the turmoil situation on the client PC market earlier. In fact, back in the early 2000s, when Intel was led by Craig Barrett, the company routinely issued mid-quarter business updates to inform investors about changes in its financial outlook. In fact, in September 2004, Intel used such an update to cut its third-quarter revenue and gross margin projections due to weaker-than-expected demand for its processors and inventory adjustments by its customers, which were very similar circumstances that the company faced in the third quarter of 2026.

A similar update could have alerted Intel's shareholders to the challenges the chipmaker faced well ahead of its quarterly earnings release. Unfortunately, Intel abandoned the practice of mid-quarter updates in January 2006 under Paul Otellini, though it occasionally revised its guidance between quarterly earnings releases thereafter, particularly during the global financial crisis of 2008 – 2010.

Intel's shareholders also allege that the company had a financial incentive to withhold information about the state of its business as it raised $23 billion through a stock offering at $95 per share in mid-August, roughly halfway through its third quarter. Intel secured the additional capital as it planned to expand its semiconductor production capacity.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Intel’s stock price dropped by 28.6% on October 30, erasing around $140 billion of the company's market capitalization, after the chipmaker issued Q4 revenue and earnings projections that fell short of expectations and warned that the PC market downturn would persist. Meanwhile, despite the massive sell-off, Intel's shares have gained 62% since the beginning of the year.

The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages on behalf of Intel investors who purchased the company's shares between July 23 and October 29, 2026. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan and CFO David Zinsner are also named as defendants.

#10296. Slack and Teams have a neurotypical bias. Here’s how to fix it

Text-based workplace communication platforms like Slack, Teams and email can create challenges for neurodiverse workers. But most have easy fixes—and the solutions can benefit all workers.

According to an analysis by BRYGE AI, an online tool that helps make messages more neurodiverse friendly, most workers fail to recognize the ways in which their communication style poses challenges for recipients with autism, ADHD, dyslexia, or other neurological or learning differences.  

For example, research suggests that it takes most people an average of over 23 minutes to return to a task after being interrupted, and that workers are interrupted every two minutes by an email, meeting or notification. Getting back on track, however, can be especially difficult for those with ADHD, who often struggle with task paralysis, executive dysfunction and a more fragile working memory.

“Slack and Teams have the green dot, there are typing bubbles, read receipts, received and sent signals, all built into it—so now, there’s an implicit pressure to respond right away,” explains BRYGE AI founder and AI engineering lead for Uptrend Motion, Rebecca Koniahgari. “We took these flexible tools and turned them into a stopwatch, where everybody is being judged by visibility.”

Working across communication channels can also make it hard for anyone—but especially neurodiverse workers—to find a needle in a haystack of information. When answers are not easy to find, or when requests are not made explicit, those with autism or ADHD can quickly become overwhelmed.

“Messages get spread across different channels—email, DMs, Slack, Teams, iMessage, WhatsApp—and nobody knows where the decision was made,” Koniahgari says. “Sometimes you don’t respond because you don’t know what it is the other person is asking. And then they read it as ‘this person’s a no-show’ or is disengaged.”

Workplace communication tools can also create what Koniahgari calls “urgency ambiguity,” which occurs when a message inadvertently creates panic due to its lack of detail, such as a “Can we talk?” message from a manager. “One person reads it as, ‘Great, we’re going to have a good conversation later.’ And another person thinks they’re getting fired,” she says.

Text-based communication platforms also often lack the richness of context that comes with real-world interactions, leaving recipients to fill in the blanks on their own.  

“For neurodivergent people, there are a lot of gaps that need to be filled in to understand what a message means. All this ambiguity adds to the cognitive load,” Koniahgari says. “Now they have to manage the extra invisible cognitive load on top of the real work that they have to do.”

Why bridging the gap often falls on neurodiverse workers

The switch from mostly real-world to more online and asynchronous workplace communication hasn’t been all bad for neurodiverse workers.

For example, ADHD workers, who often struggle with short-term memory, can search through past conversations for information they can’t recall, while autistic workers who struggle with eye contact may find it more comfortable to communicate by text.  

At the same time, Koniahgari says online platforms also inherited the broader workplace expectation that communication practices default to neurotypical norms, putting the onus on the neurodiverse workers to adjust their approach. That is what autistic sociologist and social psychologist Dr. Damian Milton refers to as the “double-empathy problem.”

The theory, Dr. Milton says, was developed in response to accusations that those with autism lack social skills, which he believes is only true when considered through a neurotypical lens. Those perceived communication shortfalls, he says, often disintegrate when the same individual is interacting with autistic peers.

“Breakdowns can happen between any two people. However, in the autistic/non-autistic setting, the autistic person is constructed as being impaired,” he explains. “This can often lead to autistic voices being devalued.”

Communication breakdowns, he suggests, are more common between groups or individuals whose brains are wired differently. Yet only the autistic group is believed to lack communication skills.

Dr. Milton adds that the same is true in the workplace, as the onus typically falls on the neurodiverse worker to adapt to a more neurotypical communication style. According to a study by neurodiversity non-profit Understood.org, 69% of neurodivergent men and 75% of neurodivergent women feel pressure to conform to neurotypical behaviors at work.

While the double empathy problem has been primarily studied in the context of autism, Dr. Milton says he believes it would also be applicable to other forms of neurodiversity.

Finding fixes that work for everyone

Small changes to how we use workplace communication tools can make a significant difference for neurodiverse employees by reducing their cognitive load, removing unnecessary distractions and making instructions and tasks easier to follow.

“There’s such an easy fix: just add a few words,” says Sarah Greenberg, a licensed psychotherapist for neurodivergence nonprofit Understood.org. “It doesn’t take very long, and it can make such a difference in someone’s day. Like instead of ‘Can we talk?’ say, ‘Do you have time to talk? It’s not urgent. A question just came up that I think you’re the best person to answer. Let me know if you have time before tomorrow.’”

Providing a clear subject for the conversation, a clear timeline and some added context can turn a message that might derail someone’s day into the innocuous request it was intended to be.

“I would rather have my team focus on the important work that we’ve hired them to do than have them spend their time twisting and turning to try to translate what it is I mean,” Greenberg adds.

A little extra effort at the outset can also help reduce the overwhelmed feeling that can result from having information scattered across platforms and conversations.

“Accessibility is strongest when it is informed by lived experience. By bringing neurodivergent perspectives into product development, Microsoft can better understand where experiences may unintentionally exclude users, learn from diverse ways of thinking and working, and create solutions that ultimately benefit a much broader audience,” says Neil Barnett, Microsoft’s Chief Accessibility Officer. (Fast Company also reached out to Slack for comment, but didn’t hear back by time of publication.)

“When we create space for neurodivergent voices to shape our products, we don’t just improve accessibility, we build better technology for everyone,” Barnett’s statement continues.

Simple strategies, like starting a long message with the ultimate request or assignment rather than burying it within, making key details explicit, numbering points or questions to be answered or addressed in sequence, including supporting materials or clear instructions on where to find them can all go a long way.

Furthermore, giving workers permission to disappear from the Slack or Teams channel while engaged in their work, and designating a clear protocol for managing actual emergencies, can also help reduce distractions for all workers.

“One of the best things you could do as a leader—and certainly as a leader of neurodivergent individuals—is being really clear on what the goal is and when it’s needed,” Greenberg says. “If you can do that consistently, it will make a huge difference.”

Nov. 17, 12:45 p.m. ET: This story was updated to include a comment from Microsoft.

#10293. People’s AI secrets raise questions about the use of chatbots in personal life

A purple box set up on a folding table in San Francisco’s Alamo Square could have been mistaken for a tissue box. Instead, it held dozens of secrets.

Olivia Tai was nearby, watching as passersby puzzled over a sign that read, “Confession box: Everyone has an AI secret.”

Among confessions about farming out too much work or using artificial intelligence to suggest a first-date spot were several admissions about using it to write deeply personal messages: “I had AI write my breakup text.” “I had ChatGPT date my boyfriend. Every text.” “I used AI to write my girlfriend’s grandmother’s 80th birthday letter.”

“I used AI to win an argument. Lol, not proud, but I won.”

Tai, an artist who has repeated the project more than a dozen times in the Bay Area, New York and Denver, said calling it a “confession” suggested people were admitting that using AI made them feel at least a little guilty. But they used it anyway.

As more people turn to a chatbot to write emails or handle mundane tasks, it raises the question: Does using it for personal messages cross a line? Is it ever OK to use AI to write a holiday card or birthday message? What about a love letter or wedding vows?

Some use AI to write personal messages, even if they feel guilty about it

As part of research for a Ph.D. in consumer behavior, Danielle Hass conducted vignette-based experiments to determine how people felt about using AI to write personal messages. She found that people who had used AI before felt just as guilty as those who hadn’t.

“Everyone felt guilty,” said Hass, a professor at Kennesaw State University in Georgia. “The driver of this relationship was dishonesty, that people felt like they were manipulating.”

Even if people are honest about their AI use, others still view them negatively, said Scott Claessens, a senior researcher at the University of Bristol in the UK.

Claessens says his research suggests that people who use AI are perceived as lazier, less competent and less trustworthy.

He noted that people often already supplement social tasks, such as using pre-written birthday cards or poems in love notes. But something about the effortless way that AI works turns people off, he said.

“What we really want in our social relationships is for people to put effort in, because it shows that as a signal that you’re invested in the relationship,” he said.

How to know when it’s not OK to use AI

Sarah Newman, who collaborated with Tai as director of art and education at Harvard University’s metaLAB, said AI adoption is happening so quickly that norms will likely emerge about when it’s appropriate and when it’s not.

She suggested using conflicted feelings as a guide. If you imagine using AI to write your wedding vows, would you be comfortable telling your partner you used it? If not, then don’t.

“Personal messages don’t need to be perfect,” Newman said. “Part of what makes these messages authentic and endearing is that they are imperfect.”

Tai and Claessens said some situations could warrant using AI in personal situations, such as people in relationships who use it to communicate better with a partner who doesn’t share a native language. People with learning disabilities, such as dyslexia, could also use it for help.

Hass believes people are quickly accepting that AI can make them more efficient in some work contexts, but she said she’s glad people feel guilty using it for personal messages.

“Guilt’s purpose in this context is to show us our interpersonal wrongdoings,” Hass said. “It’s showing us, ‘hey, this is where you’re supposed to be human.'”

Albert Stumm writes about travel, food and wellness. Find his work at https://www.albertstumm.com

—Albert Stumm, Associated Press

It needs no PC and no internet, just a console running GoldHEN.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Developer Leonardo Alegría’s open-source project Garlic LLM lets a jailbroken PS4 run the 9-billion-parameter Qwen3.5-9B AI model offline on the console’s 2013-era GPU. The app talks to the GPU directly, and the model is shrunk to about 4.5GiB to fit in the console’s memory, running at 31 to 39 tokens per second.

The project, named after the memory the GPU reads directly — its sibling memory type is “Onion” — relies on a PS4 running GoldHEN, which is a homebrew enabler for exploited consoles. Garlic LLM is a free, single 5.66GB download, available on Hugging Face and installable through the PS4’s Package Installer, with about 6GB free needed, or 12GB if the package is first copied to the console’s internal disk. The developer tested it on a base/Slim PS4 on firmware 11.52.

It’s capable of voice conversation, with spoken replies in seven languages through the Chatterbox speech model and the chat model running at about 22 tokens per second. A held controller button also lets it take dictation with Nvidia’s Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 speech-to-text model, which supports 25 European languages. Parakeet models also power local transcription and dictation apps such as Meetily and Hex. The main model is Alibaba’s small open-weight Qwen3.5-9B, which, at the claimed 31 to 39 tokens per second in text chat — the prompt and test method are not given — is usable on the console.

The closest comparison is the PS5LM fork, which runs llama.cpp as a native app on the PS5 and reaches the console’s AMD GPU through PS5_Vulkan, a port of the RADV driver. The open-source llama.cpp is a widely used program for running language models locally, and RADV is the open-source driver that lets AMD GPUs run Vulkan, the graphics and compute API. On the PS4 there is no such driver layer for homebrew; Garlic LLM uses neither llama.cpp nor a Vulkan port, or so it would appear.

The model’s operations, such as matrix multiplies over 4-bit weights, are compute kernels written in OpenCL C and compiled with LLVM for AMD’s Graphics Core Next (GCN) architecture. The weights are kept in that “Garlic” memory, while the CPU side, in plain C, handles the tokenizer, the interface, text rendering, and audio. The pipeline runs from the prompt to the CPU tokenizer, then, for each token, a PM4 command buffer — the low-level commands a graphics driver would normally generate, which, in this case, the app builds itself — and the GCN kernels, before the token is displayed or spoken. The whole thing is built with the open-source OpenOrbis PS4 toolchain.

One immediate question is how you fit a 9-billion-parameter model in the console’s 8GB of memory, which the CPU and GPU share. At 8 bits per weight, you have one byte per parameter, meaning you’d need at least 9GB, with typically more than that required overall. Part of the answer is 4-bit (“Q4”) weights, which take half as much, although 3-bit (“Q3”) weights, at about 3.5 bits with scales, are used for the two largest matrices in each layer.

Using the combination gets you to about 4.5GiB, versus about 4.9GiB if it were all 4-bit. The attention, or KV, cache is also 4-bit, which lets a 16K-token context fit, in comparison to the model’s native 256K. The Parakeet dictation model adds 0.33GiB and the Chatterbox voice models 0.29GiB and 0.09GiB, for a grand total of 5.23GiB, or 5.62GB, which closely matches the 5.66GB package size.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The next question is performance. Qwen3.5 comes with a multi-token prediction (MTP) head, and Garlic LLM uses it to draft up to two tokens ahead, with the full model verifying. This matches what the model was trained for, and the vLLM instructions on Alibaba’s model card use two speculative tokens. The project credits this for its chat speed on 2013 hardware.

Code also comes out faster with this setup, at up to 43 tokens per second. Also detailed is the default temperature, or model variability, which is 0.7 — Alibaba recommends 0.7 for general tasks with thinking off and 1.0 with it on — although the demo video uses 0, so it is predictable. At 35 tokens per second, the middle of the reported performance range, a 300-token answer takes under nine seconds. As a comparison, the PS5 ran the three-times-larger Qwen3.8-27B at about 20 tokens per second and the smaller Gemma 4 E4B and Llama 3.2 3B at 61 and 124, respectively, which is potentially quicker.

The PS4 Pro is “not tested yet,” but the developer is asking users for reports on GitHub. The PS5 is not supported as the app is written specifically for the PS4’s GPU and system software. The app itself contains no exploit, but GoldHEN is installed at the user’s own risk.

#10290. Inside Hank Green’s plan to protect kids (and their parents) from YouTube

Pity the parent trying to pull the plug on YouTube, Netflix, or Disney Plus mid-video. The tears! The world-ending wails! 

Hank Green, host of popular YouTube channels Crash Course and SciShow, has been that parent. A longtime science educator and the co-creator of VidCon, Green has fought his fair share of “turn it off” battles with his son. 

“These systems are designed to keep kids watching,” he says of advertising-based platforms like YouTube and TikTok. “They don’t have any incentives to even consider designing a ‘stop’ experience.”

But parents, on the other hand, are highly incentivized to seek out an alternative to the endless scroll of sometimes questionable content that streams to family devices. Green hopes they will give his new venture, ClockwiseTV, a chance. 

Launching publicly today, ClockwiseTV is a subscription-based app featuring curated creator videos for kids ages 8-12. Parents establish a session length when opening the app; once kids start watching, ClockwiseTV helps them pick a video sequence that concludes when their session concludes. 

The app’s constrained choice philosophy extends to the video selection experience. Instead of infinite options, ClockwiseTV presents kids with a menu of just a dozen videos at a time, based on their interests (animals, space, history, etc). Each video has been vetted by a human and scrubbed of any inappropriate language. Creators in the initial library include Animal Wonders Montana, NerdForge, Crash Course Kids, and MinuteEarth. 

At launch, a subscription costs $6.99 a month or $69.99 a year. There are no ads, and the app is compliant with the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act, or COPPA. 

No autoplay, no rabbit holes

ClockwiseTV joins a growing array of products designed to keep kids entertained without algorithms or ads. For screen-free audio content, there are Yoto players and Tonie boxes. For kids who want to gab with their besties, there is the Tin Can phone, which mimics the experience of a landline for an approved set of friends and family. There are even sticker printers that use AI to turn kids’ ideas into black-and-white stickers they can color and decorate. 

Green says he’s been working on ClockwiseTV for about a year. The decision to focus on tweens stems from his own experience as a parent. “My son is this age, so that’s part of it,” he says. “There’s a kind of no-man’s-land of content where it’s like, you’re done with Mr. Rogers, here’s all of YouTube. I think that’s probably not the right way to do it.” 

Over time, he adds, ClockwiseTV may pursue “other slices of the pie” and expand its target audience. 

More than half of children own a smartphone by age 11, according to Common Sense Media’s 2026 census. The average tween spends five hours a day watching entertainment on a screen, the census found. 

Leslie Morgan, who has worked in digital media with creators for more than a decade, joined ClockwiseTV as CEO in January. Like Green, she hopes to help parents avoid the internet’s darker corners. “There are no rabbit holes, there’s no autoplay,” Morgan says of the app. 

Incentivizing kid-friendly creators

ClockwiseTV is paying creators to license their content. “A lot of these creators would love to get in front of a younger audience, and it’s not financially viable,” says Morgan, explaining that labeling content as “made for kids” on YouTube typically lowers creators’ AdSense revenue. “For them, it doesn’t make economic sense.” With ClockwiseTV, she argues, creators can access new audiences and supplement their income from other platforms. 

When I watch YouTube with my kids, it’s often a stressful experience. Typically they’ve requested to revisit a favorite video that, in their view, is very specific (“the tap dancing man in the hat!”). It’s up to me to weed through a confounding list of thumbnails and keyword-optimized titles, searching for an elusive winner, while they squirm impatiently. 

ClockwiseTV, in contrast, is built to reward parental trust. I told the app that my son was interested in history videos, and had just 15 minutes to watch. The app suggested a short video about fossils and a slightly longer video about hunting for 50 million-year-old shark teeth. Both were educational and engaging. 

“That’s it for now,” the app announced when the allotted time was up. “Go do something else that’s awesome!” 

I found myself wishing that Instagram would tell me the same thing.

#10288. I’d rather use Android XR glasses over Meta Ray-Bans for the app alone

In trying out Google’s Intelligent Eyewear Android XR glasses for the first time, one of my main takeaways is that it’s the app, not necessarily the glasses themselves that would push me into using them over the mainstay Meta Ray-Bans.

One of the inherent advantages that Android XR glasses were always going to have over third-party options is native integration. It’s something we see frequently, and perhaps most well-known on smartwatches.

The “Glasses” app on Android/Pixel, iOS, and Samsung Galaxy devices is dead simple. While we can’t show you the full app just yet as the one we were able to try was not completely final, it’s a very simple experience.

The app opens to an overview of your glasses to show their connection and battery status, with settings below for Gemini, apps, the camera, and more. You’ll also be able to see things such as what the various lights on the glasses mean, tutorials, and more. There’s no bloat and no messing around – it’s a utility to just make adjustments or control the glasses as needed.

You’ll probably be using this app mostly to view the photos and videos captured on Android XR glasses. Google has this set up to auto-import photos in nearly real-time. It only takes about 4 seconds to import and the process starts immediately for photos. Videos, on the other hand, take longer and may need to be manually imported (for the sake of battery in part, Google mentioned).

Across the three main platforms, there are some differences. The iPhone app doesn’t import photos quite as fast, and Samsung has its own app to fit in with One UI’s design language for Galaxy users, but the core premise is the same across all three.

While we’ll have to see how this works in real life, I was blown away by how simple it all was, though that might be because the bar is below the floor.

Meta’s Ray-Bans (and newer Meta Glasses) dominate the smart glasses conversation, and I think that the app is one of the biggest problems. It’s certainly one of the biggest reasons I’ve barely touched my Wayfarers in recent months. That’s because, in early 2025, Meta replaced its dedicated “View” app for its glasses with a Meta AI app, which is just invasive and distasteful in my book. Meta is no stranger to shoving AI down the throat of its existing users. Another well-known move was converting Facebook and Instagram search into AI search boxes with creepy levels of context and invasive actions – it makes Google’s AI Overviews look tame by comparison. But I’d argue the most aggressive was this move with its glasses. Something as simple as tweaking a setting or importing a photo now forces you to dodge an AI chatbot.

Truly, Meta’s app is the worst, and I applaud Google for building a very simple utility for Android XR glasses instead.
